structured_output.hypothesis: Troglobitic (cave-restricted) species sampled in North America and in Europe are placed taxonomically within the surface-dwelling lineages of their own continent, so cave species from the two continents rarely share genera or families that are absent from the other continent's surface fauna.
structured_output.pass_criterion: Among GBIF occurrence records of cave-restricted species (identified by habitat or locality text such as 'cave' or 'cavern' and the stygobiont/troglobiont keywords, then curated to confirmed obligate cave species) in a North American box and a European box, at least 80% of the cave genera in each continent also have at least one surface-dwelling (non-cave) congener or confamilial species recorded on the same continent. In addition, the share of cave genera found on both continents must be under 10% of all cave genera.
structured_output.fail_criterion: Fewer than 60% of the cave genera on either continent have a same-continent surface relative at genus or family level, or 25% or more of cave genera are shared between the continents (a cave fauna that is more alike across continents than within each continent's fauna).
structured_output.interpretation: 'Blind cave animals' are read as obligate cave-dwelling (troglobiont and stygobiont) species, whether or not they are blind. 'Affinities' and 'allied' are read as shared genus or family in the GBIF backbone taxonomy, with a same-continent surface relative as the criterion. 'America' is read as North America for sampling; Darwin's example was the Kentucky Mammoth Cave. This is a modern taxonomic proxy for his morphological judgement of affinity. Occurrence records do not label a species as cave-restricted, so the cave set must be curated by a habitat keyword filter plus expert checking. This is a limitation of the test.

dataset.name: GBIF Occurrence Download / Occurrence Search API (GBIF.org)
dataset.why_it_fits: GBIF's occurrence search API is public and returned a count of about 3.89 billion records. Fields that could be used: scientificName, genus, family, order, countryCode, decimalLatitude and decimalLongitude, continent, habitat and locality text, and the kingdom and phylum filters. These allow classifying cave records and checking whether each genus has surface congeners on the same continent. The GBIF website itself returned HTTP 403 to my fetch, so only the API endpoint was verified.
